claims.text: Specific elemental composition governs the structural stability of high-entropy nanoalloys at high temperature.
Specific elemental composition governs the chemical stability of high-entropy nanoalloys at high temperature.
Composition controls stability by modulating lattice distortion.
Greater lattice distortion raises local energy barriers for atomic diffusion.
Higher diffusion barriers caused by lattice distortion reduce surface segregation.
Higher diffusion barriers caused by lattice distortion reduce phase instability.
Differences in constituent elemental atomic radii produce lattice distortion.
The comparison will use initially single-phase high-entropy nanoalloys with controlled compositions and different atomic-size mismatches.
The experiment will vary elemental composition and examine the alloys by in situ high-temperature TEM and EDS at 700–1000°C under an inert atmosphere.
Using an inert atmosphere isolates composition-dependent behavior from oxidation effects.
Compositions with lower lattice distortion have higher atomic mobility.
Higher atomic mobility in low-distortion compositions leads to greater surface segregation.
Higher atomic mobility in low-distortion compositions leads to structural instability.
High-distortion nanoalloys will exhibit less surface segregation than near-equiatomic, low-distortion baseline alloys during high-temperature exposure.
High-distortion nanoalloys will retain a more compositionally uniform crystal structure than the baseline alloys.
Near-equiatomic baseline compositions induce minimal lattice distortion.
Oxidation-related degradation may dominate stability behavior under oxidizing conditions.
Local chemical ordering or impurities may also affect stability.
Failure of the high-distortion alloys to show reduced segregation and improved structural stability relative to the baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
